issues.subcategory: inconsistent coding of frequency scales
issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently reports the coding range for the same frequency measures. In the main Methods text, pornography frequency is described as scored 1–6, whereas the supplemental table shows 0–5, matching the ASSIST-style coding. This inconsistency affects inclusion thresholds, centering, interaction construction, and reproducibility.
issues.quote: "Pornography viewing frequency will be assessed using the same modified frequency scale as is present on the ASSIST, wherein participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)."

issues.subcategory: contradictory inclusion rule tied to inconsistent coding
issues.description: The inclusion criterion for pornography users depends on the inconsistent scale coding. If the scale is 0–5, scores >1 imply monthly or more, not 'at least once in the past 12 months.' If the scale is 1–6, scores >1 would indicate at least once or twice. This directly changes which participants are analyzed and can bias results.
issues.quote: "only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months (i.e., scores > 1 on the frequency measure) will complete the remaining items described below."

issues.subcategory: number of outcomes does not match stated analyses
issues.description: The manuscript states there are eight proposed outcomes, then later states there will be 10 moderation analyses corresponding to '8 target behaviors/variables of interest,' with pornography and gambling repeated. Table 1 lists 7 target rows, not 8. These discrepancies make the analytic plan unclear and raise concern that analyses are not fully specified.
issues.quote: "Prior to our primary analyses, assumptions of regression ... will be tested for each of the eight proposed outcomes." ... "In total, we will conduct 10 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest"

issues.subcategory: gambling frequency measure described inconsistently
issues.description: In one place gambling frequency is described as a single item, but elsewhere the manuscript states that an average across gambling behaviors will be taken. The supplement appears to include one item asking about any gambling behavior, not multiple items that could be averaged. This inconsistency undermines clarity about how the predictor is constructed.
issues.quote: "We will assess gambling frequency using a single item." ... "To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken."

issues.subcategory: alcohol item wording inconsistency by gender
issues.description: The supplemental materials state the male branching item asks about 'more than 5 drinks,' but the displayed row label says 'More than four drinks (1).' This is an internal inconsistency in the instrument wording and could induce implementation or scoring errors.
issues.quote: "IF GENDER = MAN ... In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion? ... More than four drinks (1)"

issues.subcategory: incorrect claim about Holm-adjusted test statistics
issues.description: Holm correction adjusts p-values or decision thresholds, not the underlying correlation 'test statistics.' Reporting 'Holm-adjusted test statistics' is statistically incorrect and suggests confusion about multiple-testing correction.
issues.quote: "Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package."

issues.subcategory: use of OLS for ordinal/count-like outcomes without clear justification
issues.description: Primary analyses are specified as ordinary least squares moderation models despite outcomes being sums/averages of ordinal items with bounded distributions and likely skew, floor effects, and non-normality. The plan mentions assumption checks, but OLS is still the default and latent-variable analyses are only supplemental if assumptions are 'substantially violated.' This is especially problematic for low-base-rate substances and for scale sums like BPS and PGSI.
issues.quote: "As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software"

issues.subcategory: equivalence region based on incomparable metric
issues.description: The equivalence bound for a regression interaction is set using a standardized beta from prior studies, but the manuscript simultaneously references ΔR2, f2, and Cohen's d as if they are interchangeable indicators of the same SESOI. These metrics are not directly commensurate, especially for interaction terms in multivariable models. This undermines the justification for δ=.11.
issues.quote: "we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen’s d = .25"

issues.subcategory: post hoc redefinition of equivalence bounds
issues.description: The plan explicitly states that if initial equivalence tests fail, the equivalence region will be redefined using the observed pornography effect in the current data. This is circular and invalidates the confirmatory status of the equivalence tests by making the decision rule outcome-dependent.
issues.quote: "In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence ... we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome."

issues.subcategory: outcome-contingent analytic switching
issues.description: The manuscript allows switching from OLS to latent variable modeling based on observed assumption violations and then choosing which results to foreground if signs/significance remain similar. This creates substantial analytic flexibility because the precise threshold for 'substantial' violation and criteria for robustness are unspecified.
issues.quote: "in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses ... Should results of moderation analyses remain robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same across analytic techniques), we will present OLS results"

issues.subcategory: unspecified supplemental robustness analyses
issues.description: The plan states supplemental analyses will be conducted 'as appropriate' when assumptions are violated, without pre-specifying which diagnostics trigger which remedies. This leaves considerable undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: "in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate."

issues.subcategory: unclear handling of multiple confirmatory tests
issues.description: The study proposes 10 moderation analyses plus correlations and possible supplementary latent models, but no familywise error control or false discovery control is specified for the primary hypothesis tests. This increases the risk of false positives, especially given domain-by-domain testing and dual outcomes for pornography and gambling.
issues.quote: "In total, we will conduct 10 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency"

issues.subcategory: nonparallel and noncomparable measurement across domains
issues.description: The central theoretical claim compares moral incongruence across pornography, gambling, and substances, but the outcomes are measured using different instruments, different response ranges, different time windows, and different content coverage across domains (e.g., BPS 6 months, PGSI 12 months, modified ASSIST problems 3 months). Cross-domain comparisons of interaction magnitude are therefore not cleanly interpretable as reflecting domain differences rather than measurement differences.
issues.quote: "In total, we will conduct 10 moderation analyses ... with pornography and gambling repeated for both the NIDA-ASSIST measure and the validate measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively)."

issues.subcategory: mismatch between moral incongruence construct and operationalization
issues.description: The manuscript defines moral incongruence as the interaction between moral disapproval and behavior frequency. However, incongruence conceptually refers to discrepancy between values and behavior, which is not equivalent to a multiplicative term. A person with high disapproval and low use may be highly incongruent, whereas the product term is low. Conversely, high use and moderate disapproval can produce a large product without clear subjective incongruence. This operationalization may not validly capture the target construct.
issues.quote: "moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior)"

issues.subcategory: single-item measurement of moral disapproval
issues.description: Moral disapproval is treated as a central moderator yet is assessed with a single item for each domain. Single items are vulnerable to unreliability and may conflate moral wrongness with legality, health concerns, social stigma, or religious norms, especially for substances. Measurement error in a moderator also attenuates interaction effects and complicates comparisons across domains.
issues.quote: "Additionally, we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions ... 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong'"

issues.subcategory: outcome contamination by guilt item
issues.description: The Brief Pornography Screen includes an item about guilt ('You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it'), which conceptually overlaps with moral disapproval and moral incongruence. This can inflate the association between moral disapproval and the pornography outcome, creating a nonparallel advantage for pornography relative to outcomes in other domains.
issues.quote: "5. You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it."

issues.subcategory: PGSI includes guilt item overlapping with moral disapproval
issues.description: The Problem Gambling Severity Index also includes guilt, meaning the gambling outcome similarly contains an evaluative/moral-affective component. Because outcomes differ in the extent and type of overlap with moral disapproval, cross-domain interaction comparisons remain confounded by measure content.
issues.quote: "Have you felt guilty about the way you gamble or what happens when you gamble?"

issues.subcategory: modified ASSIST extended to nonvalidated behaviors
issues.description: The ASSIST was designed for substance involvement screening. The manuscript adds gambling and pornography items to create 'fully parallel analysis,' but explicitly acknowledges these extensions are not validated. Lack of validation means differences across domains may reflect instrument artifacts rather than substantive differences in moral incongruence.
issues.quote: "We will also include pornography and gambling as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST ... Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography"

issues.subcategory: alteration of validated alcohol screening item changes meaning
issues.description: The NIDA Quick Screen alcohol item is modified from binge-threshold frequency to any alcohol frequency, materially changing the construct from risky drinking to general consumption. This undermines comparability with the ASSIST framework and with moral disapproval of alcohol use, and may weaken or distort associations with problem indicators.
issues.quote: "for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed)."

issues.subcategory: collapsing heterogeneous nicotine products into one item
issues.description: Combining cigarettes, smokeless tobacco, and vaping into a single frequency item obscures qualitatively different behaviors with different moral meanings, legal statuses, and use patterns. This weakens construct validity for both frequency and disapproval, and compromises comparability with a separate table entry for 'Tobacco/Nicotine products.'
issues.quote: "we will make it explicitly clear that smoked tobacco products, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless tobacco products are all subsumed by our single question on tobacco/nicotine."

issues.subcategory: combining legal cannabis and illicit drugs into broad categories
issues.description: The study measures 'Cannabis/Marijuana/THC' and separately 'Illegal/Illicit Drugs,' but both categories remain broad and heterogeneous. Moral disapproval likely differs sharply by specific substance, route, legal context, and medical use. Single broad categories may not validly capture the targeted moral-behavior discrepancy construct.
issues.quote: "we will add cannabis/THC related products to our focal substances, as it is commonly used but may no longer be considered illicit or illegal in many regions."

issues.subcategory: conditioning on behavior induces selection bias
issues.description: Moral disapproval and problem measures are only administered to those who report past-year engagement in a behavior. Restricting analyses to users may induce collider bias because both disapproval and risk factors can influence whether one engages at all. It also excludes individuals with strong disapproval who abstain, despite their relevance to the broader construct of incongruence and to prevalence estimates.
issues.quote: "we will only administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to participants who report engaging in those behaviors."

issues.subcategory: mismatched recall windows between predictors and outcomes
issues.description: Behavior frequency is assessed over the past 12 months, whereas modified ASSIST problems are past 3 months, BPS is last 6 months, and PGSI is last 12 months. Interaction effects between moral disapproval and frequency therefore pair predictors and outcomes drawn from different time windows, complicating interpretation and threatening internal validity.
issues.quote: "participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months" ... "In the past three months" ... "In the last 6 months" ... "Thinking about the last 12 months"

issues.subcategory: oversample not accounted for in representativeness claim
issues.description: The total sample includes a 1,500-person oversample of sports wagerers, yet analyses appear to pool the national sample and oversample. Without a weighting plan or separate analyses, pooled estimates are not representative of the U.S. population and may distort gambling-related associations and covariate relationships.
issues.quote: "This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults."

issues.subcategory: no weighting plan for YouGov matched sample and oversample
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the design as nationally representative but does not specify whether YouGov post-stratification weights will be used, how the sports-betting oversample will be weighted, or whether analyses will be design-adjusted. Without this information, population-level inference is not evaluable.
issues.quote: "Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms."

issues.subcategory: overclaim of representative inference from pooled nonprobability panel plus oversample
issues.description: The manuscript speaks of a representative U.S. sample and population-level conclusions, but the final analytic sample includes a nonprobability panel matched to norms plus a purposive sports-betting oversample. Without weighting and design details, claims about the 'American public' or U.S. prevalence/generalizability are overstated.
issues.quote: "the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms ... we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports"

issues.subcategory: gender coding is exclusionary and inconsistent
issues.description: Gender is included as a binary covariate with '1 = male, and 0 = not-male,' despite the use of panel data where gender categories may be more complex. This coding collapses women and nonbinary participants, reducing interpretability and potentially biasing estimates if gender effects differ across groups.
issues.quote: "Interactions will be tested using this program with gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)"

issues.subcategory: lack of exact model specifications for each outcome
issues.description: The manuscript does not provide explicit regression equations, whether coefficients will be standardized or unstandardized in confirmatory tests, or whether interaction plots/simple slopes will be estimated at fixed values. This omission hampers reproducibility, especially because equivalence testing is tied to a standardized effect metric.
issues.quote: "We will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function"

issues.subcategory: unclear treatment of survey branching and skipped items
issues.description: Because only users complete downstream items, and some alcohol items are gender-conditional, there is implicit planned missingness. The manuscript nevertheless claims there will be 'no unplanned missingness' and does not specify data structures, coding of structurally missing values, or how these will be distinguished from item nonresponse.
issues.quote: "Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data."

issues.subcategory: missing data assumptions unrealistic and unaddressed
issues.description: The plan assumes no unplanned missingness because of YouGov data collection standards, but panel surveys still typically contain item nonresponse, dropoff, or implausible/partial completion. No plan is given for handling any missing data if it occurs (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation). This is especially problematic given subgroup analyses with rare behaviors.
issues.quote: "Accordingly, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data."

issues.subcategory: standardizing and averaging heterogeneous ASSIST items
issues.description: The problematic-use index averages z-standardized responses from items with different response formats, time frames, and meaning. Standardization is sample-dependent and can obscure interpretability, especially across behaviors with different prevalence and variance. It also complicates comparability of effect sizes across domains, because each outcome metric is partly determined by sample distribution rather than scale content alone.
issues.quote: "Responses to each of the above five items will be standardized, and an average will be taken for each substance of interest"

issues.subcategory: problematic-use composite conflates distinct constructs
issues.description: The five ASSIST-based items include urge, consequences, functional impairment, others' concern, and failed control. Combining these via standardized averaging without validation assumes a unidimensional latent construct of 'addiction/problematic use' across all domains, including pornography and gambling. This may not hold and threatens construct validity.
issues.quote: "To assess problematic or potentially addictive use of these substances, we will take the average of responses to problematic use questions present in the NIDA-ASSIST."

issues.subcategory: low-powered rare-substance subgroup analyses
issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges very low projected Ns for prescription misuse and illicit drugs, yet still frames substance analyses as tests of uniqueness. With projected n≈140 for prescription misuse and 240–480 for illicit drugs, interaction estimates and equivalence tests will be unstable, and null findings may be uninformative.
issues.quote: "Prescription Drug Misuse | 3.5% | 140 ... Estimated Achieved power for f2= .015 .301"

issues.subcategory: equivalence testing underpowered for key null claims
issues.description: The core claims for gambling/substances rely on equivalence to a practically zero interaction, yet Table 2 shows inadequate power for some substances to detect the prespecified smallest effect. Underpowered equivalence tests cannot support the intended null-type conclusions about nonuniqueness versus uniqueness.
issues.quote: "it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small"

issues.subcategory: fallback to less stringent comparison when equivalence not testable
issues.description: When power is insufficient for equivalence to zero, the authors propose testing whether effects are smaller than a relatively large pornography benchmark. This substantially weakens the confirmatory claim while retaining an appearance of hypothesis testing, and it changes the inferential target after seeing feasibility constraints.
issues.quote: "Should we lack power to sufficient test equivalence with null effects ... we will test an alternative model where our equivalence region is defined by the lower bound of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate ... β = .27"

issues.subcategory: causal language from cross-sectional associations
issues.description: Despite acknowledging the cross-sectional design, the manuscript repeatedly uses causal language such as 'influences,' 'affects,' and 'contributor' when describing expected results and implications. Cross-sectional moderation analyses cannot establish that moral incongruence causes self-perceived addiction or diagnostic inflation.
issues.quote: "we seek to establish whether moral incongruence ... influences self-perceived feelings of addiction"

issues.subcategory: unsupported diagnostic implications
issues.description: The manuscript claims that confirming the hypotheses would support the validity of ICD-11's moral-distress caveat for CSBD. However, the study uses self-report community measures, not clinician-administered diagnosis or differential diagnosis procedures. Therefore it cannot directly validate diagnostic criteria or false-positive diagnosis claims.
issues.quote: "should hypotheses be confirmed, there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD."

issues.subcategory: begged-question hypothesis framing
issues.description: The stated goal is to test whether the model generalizes beyond pornography, yet the manuscript says it aims 'with a specific goal of demonstrating' uniqueness. This wording suggests confirmatory bias rather than an even-handed test of competing explanations, which is conceptually problematic in a registered report context.
issues.quote: "with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors."

issues.subcategory: conflation of self-perceived addiction with dysregulation/disorder
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, self-reported addiction feelings, problematic use screens, compulsivity, dysregulation, and disorder symptoms are treated as near-interchangeable outcomes. These constructs are related but distinct, and the study's measures do not consistently capture clinical dysregulation. This conflation overstates what can be inferred from questionnaire associations.
issues.quote: "predict self-perceived feelings of addiction to both behaviors ... and substances" ... "predicting feelings of dysregulation" ... "self-reported gambling disorder symptoms"

issues.subcategory: insufficient distinction between morality and stigma/legality/health norms
issues.description: For substances and gambling, endorsement that a behavior is 'morally wrong' may reflect legality concerns, perceived health risk, public stigma, or social undesirability rather than personal moral disapproval. The manuscript interprets these items as morality per se, which may misapply the theoretical framework across domains.
issues.quote: "For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong'"

issues.subcategory: no information on preregistration timestamp/versioning relative to data collection
issues.description: The study is labeled a registered report and states participants will be recruited in late March 2022, but the manuscript does not clearly document whether Stage 1 approval and analysis lock occurred before any access to data, nor whether any pilot data informed the plan. This is important for evaluating confirmatory status.
issues.quote: "Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study"

issues.subcategory: insufficient details on YouGov quality-control procedures
issues.description: The authors rely on YouGov's proprietary quality standards to justify not screening for inattentive responding, but provide no details on those procedures or thresholds. Because these determine inclusion/exclusion, the lack of transparency impedes evaluation and replication.
issues.quote: "certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards."

issues.subcategory: no blinding and no mitigation of demand/social desirability bias
issues.description: The study asks respondents directly whether behaviors are morally wrong and whether they feel addicted/problematic in the same survey. This common-method, same-session self-report design is highly vulnerable to consistency motifs and social desirability bias, yet no mitigation strategy is described.
issues.quote: "Participants will also respond to ... moral disapproval questions ... [and] measures of problematic use"

issues.subcategory: pornography frequency restricted to solitary use only
issues.description: The supplemental instrument assesses pornography frequency as 'Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner),' yet the moral disapproval item refers to pornography use generally. This mismatch means the frequency term may omit partnered pornography use while the morality and outcome items do not, weakening the intended alignment of the interaction term.
issues.quote: "Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)"

issues.subcategory: table formatting errors obscure methodological details
issues.description: Table 2 and some supplemental tables contain duplicated text and formatting corruption, making it difficult to determine the exact planned values and variables. Such presentation problems reduce interpretability and can conceal specification errors.
issues.quote: "1. All substance estimates ..." repeated multiple times across Table 2

issues.subcategory: population claims despite likely exclusion of clinically relevant groups
issues.description: The sample is an online panel of adults and excludes treatment-seeking clinical populations, institutionalized individuals, and likely some populations with limited internet/panel access. Yet the discussion extends implications to diagnostic practice and clinical false positives. This extrapolation is not justified by the sample.
issues.quote: "the real potential concern associated with this effect is whether it creates false-positive diagnoses in clinical settings."

issues.subcategory: inconsistent statement about validated measures
issues.description: The manuscript says gambling and pornography will be assessed with 'validated scales' in addition to ASSIST items, but later refers to 'the validate measures' and uses averaged PGSI responses instead of the standard summed score, implying deviation from standard scoring. This inconsistency raises uncertainty about whether standard validated scoring will be used.
issues.quote: "with pornography and gambling repeated for both the NIDA-ASSIST measure and the validate measures of problematic use"

issues.subcategory: nonstandard scoring of PGSI and BPS relative to validation work
issues.description: The PGSI is described as averaged rather than summed, and the supplemental response coding appears as 0,2,4,5 rather than the standard 0,1,2,3. The BPS supplemental coding appears 0,2,4 despite the text saying 0 to 2. These discrepancies imply scoring errors or at minimum unclear scoring, which would affect comparability to validation studies and all inferential tests.
issues.quote: "problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index ... Responses will be averaged." ... supplemental: "Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)" ... "Brief Pornography Screen ... on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed." supplemental: "Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)"

issues.subcategory: no plan for survey weights in power analyses or effective N
issues.description: Effective sample sizes in Table 2 are treated as raw counts based on prevalence, but there is no indication whether design weights or oversample weighting were incorporated. If weighted analyses are used, effective N and power can differ substantially.
issues.quote: "Effective N" ... "All analyses conducted using G*power; assuming α = 0.05, regression models with 6 independent variables"
